tldr: By introducing a bidirectional antagonistic tendon-routing mechanism (BATM) that allows fingers to bend fully toward both the palmar and dorsal sides, researchers developed a human-scale, 17-DoF robotic hand capable of grasping from either side without rotating its wrist.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed bidirectional multi-fingered robotic hand. From the central neutral configuration, fingers actively flex toward both the palmar side (green) and dorsal side (red), achieving reversible dual-sided grasping that functions as both a right and left hand.
overview:
Anthropomorphic robotic hands have traditionally replicated human skeletal structures faithfully, but this means they also inherit an anatomical asymmetry: fingers only bend toward the palmar side. Consequently, grasping an object located on the opposite side requires extensive wrist or arm reorientation, introducing redundant motions and unreached blind spots.

To solve this, the authors asked a simple question: What if we kept the anthropomorphic five-digit skeleton, but made the hand symmetric so it could bend fully toward the dorsal side as well? To make this possible, they proposed the Bidirectional Antagonistic Tendon-routing Mechanism (BATM). Rather than relying on passive return springs, BATM winds two tendons in opposite directions from a single motor spool. This allows symmetric, slack-free drive in both positive and negative directions across the neutral configuration. Furthermore, by ensuring symmetric range of motion including thumb opposition and routing tendons directly through joint rotation axes (decoupling), tendon coupling across fingers and the wrist is eliminated.

The resulting prototype is compact, with a total length of 200 mm and a hand weight of around 220 g, matching human scale. Experimental evaluations demonstrated practical core performance: an average motor-to-joint transmission error of 3.0%, a transmission bandwidth of 13.2 Hz, a maximum fingertip force of 29 N, and a positioning repeatability of up to 0.15 mm after pre-stretching. It also achieved a Kapandji score of 8 and successfully reproduced all 33 grasp types of the GRASP Taxonomy on both palmar and dorsal sides.

This validates a level of manipulation flexibility that challenges conventional hand designs, enabling tasks such as catching flying objects on either side without turning the wrist and switching between right- and left-hand configurations in teleoperation using a single robotic hand.
contributions: Proposed the Bidirectional Antagonistic Tendon-routing Mechanism (BATM), which actively drives joints symmetrically in positive and negative directions across the neutral configuration from a single motor without return springs.

Established an axis-passing tendon routing layout that geometrically eliminates cross-coupling among finger flexion/extension, abduction/adduction, and wrist rotation, alongside a fully symmetric thumb opposition structure.
Realized an actual human-scale (200 mm length), lightweight (220 g hand weight), low-cost, 3D-printed 17-DoF multi-fingered robotic hand.

Demonstrated that Kapandji testing (score of 8) and all 33 GRASP Taxonomy grasp types can be achieved equally on both palmar and dorsal sides, validating dual-sided manipulation without wrist reorientation.

sections.heading: Why Do Robotic Hands Only Bend Toward the Palm?
sections.summary: This section highlights the limitations of conventional multi-fingered hands, where bending only toward the palm restricts workspace and demands redundant wrist rotation. In response, it introduces the concept of a lightweight, bidirectional tendon-driven hand capable of grasping on both sides while maintaining an anthropomorphic five-digit appearance.
sections.details:
With recent advances in Physical AI, humanoid robot development is accelerating, making dexterous hand manipulation a critical research topic. A robotic hand is not merely an end effector; it constitutes the physical body that determines interactions with the environment.

However, because many existing multi-fingered robotic hands directly replicate human anatomy, they inherit a one-sided grasping workspace where fingers bend only toward the palmar side. Grasping objects located behind or on the opposite side requires large reorientations of the arm and wrist, significantly reducing motion efficiency.

While reversible grippers and soft robotic hands capable of dual-sided grasping have been proposed before, most have few fingers or low structural stiffness, failing to qualify as human-scale, multi-DoF hands. Meanwhile, full-fledged anthropomorphic hands often embed joint gearboxes inside the fingers, making fingertips heavy and vulnerable to impacts. Tendon-driven approaches can relocate actuators to the forearm, but spring-return designs suffer from low responsiveness, while fully antagonistic setups require an excessive number of motors, driving up size and cost.

To overcome these tradeoffs, this paper proposes a 17-DoF anthropomorphic bidirectional robotic hand. By adopting joint designs with symmetric ranges of motion around the neutral configuration, non-interfering tendon routing across the neutral pose, and a symmetric thumb structure, it functions fully on both the palmar and dorsal sides without needing wrist reorientation.

sections.heading: The Routing Trick: Bending Both Ways Without Cable Slack
sections.summary: This section explains the BATM mechanism and geometric routing that actively drive both flexion and extension using a single motor across the neutral pose. Passing tendons through the rotation axes prevents multi-joint coupling while preserving a wide range of motion for thumb opposition.
sections.details:
### II-A Routing Mechanism for the Four Fingers
The core of the proposed Bidirectional Antagonistic Tendon-routing Mechanism (BATM) is that it drives joints symmetrically across the neutral configuration in both positive and negative directions. The four fingers share a modular design: three motors independently actuate MCP (metacarpophalangeal) joint flexion/extension (FE), MCP abduction/adduction (AbAd), and PIP (proximal interphalangeal) joint FE, while the DIP (distal interphalangeal) joint is mechanically coupled to the PIP joint.

Two tendons wind in opposite directions from a single motor pulley (spool) to opposite sides of a joint pulley. Turning the spool clockwise pulls one tendon while paying out the other by the exact same length. Mathematically, the change in flexion tendon length $\Delta X_{\text{flex}}$ and extension tendon length $\Delta X_{\text{ext}}$ satisfy $\Delta X_{\text{flex}} = \Delta X_{\text{ext}} = r\theta$ relative to joint radius $r$ and rotation angle $\theta$. As a result, no cable slack or excessive tension occurs when crossing the neutral position to bend in reverse. Agonist and antagonist roles swap naturally depending on the bending direction.

To prevent joint coupling in multi-DoF fingers, the MCP FE tendons pass directly through the AbAd rotation axis, while PIP FE tendons pass through both the AbAd and FE axes of the MCP joint. Tendon paths remain as straight as possible with filleted corners to minimize friction. The DIP joint is mechanically linked to the PIP joint with a 3:2 rotation ratio to generate natural, coordinated human-like motion.

### II-B Routing Mechanism for the Thumb
To achieve dexterous opposition, the thumb actively actuates all four degrees of freedom with dedicated motors: CMC (carpometacarpal) FE, CMC AbAd, MCP FE, and IP (interphalangeal) FE. BATM is employed here as well. At the CMC FE joint, a crossed tendon routing scheme is implemented to reconcile the confined palm space with an extensive opposition range ($\pm 135^{\circ}$). This wide range allows the thumb to oppose the other fingers on both the palmar and dorsal sides.

### II-C Finger Kinematics
Because the spools and joint pulleys are directly connected via tendons, the relationship between motor angles and joint angles is cleanly captured by a linear transmission matrix $\mathbf{R}$ based on pulley radius ratios. Eliminating geometric non-linearities makes joint control exceptionally straightforward.

captions.F2: Tendon routing of the proposed BATM. (a) Basic principle of winding tendons from a single spool to both sides of a joint pulley. (b) Decoupled tendon routing for the four fingers passing through joint rotation axes. (c) Crossed tendon routing for the thumb enabling a wide opposition range of $\pm 135^{\circ}$.

sections.heading: Integrating Symmetric Fingers, Palm, and Wrist Mechanisms
sections.summary: This section covers the hardware realization of BATM into an adult-male-scale (200 mm, 220 g) 3D-printed robotic hand. It details friction reduction via bearing-supported joint pulleys, a symmetric palm design, and a wrist/actuator assembly routing 32 tendons into the forearm.
sections.details:
### III-A Finger Hardware Design
The finger modules are designed after an adult male middle finger, with proximal, intermediate, and distal phalanx lengths of 44 mm, 27 mm, and 21 mm, respectively. The main frame is 3D-printed from tough PLA Tough+, and soft pads made of flexible 80A resin are mounted on contact surfaces to increase friction.

A specific challenge in BATM is that increased tendon tension causes rapid friction buildup at joint pulley contacts. To solve this, miniature bearings are embedded within the pulleys of the FE joints to ensure rolling friction. Furthermore, the pulleys feature two parallel grooves so that flexion and extension tendons do not entangle. The joint hinges are completely symmetric about the neutral position, doubling the reachable workspace across the palmar and dorsal sides.

### III-B Palm Integration
To achieve reversible dual-sided grasping, not only the skeletal frame but also the fleshy contours of the palm and dorsum are symmetric. A modular split-part structure was adopted to ease assembly and tendon routing within tight internal spaces. Adjacent fingers are arranged with a $6^{\circ}$ yaw opening angle to reproduce a human-like fan distribution. Hand weight is kept down to approximately 220 g. Including 1 DoF for the wrist, the entire hand is driven by 17 actuators.

### III-C Wrist and Actuator Module
The wrist joint has an operational range of $-60^{\circ}$ to $+60^{\circ}$. To prevent finger tendon lengths from shifting when the wrist moves, all 32 finger tendons pass through the center of the wrist rotation axis into the forearm. Spring guide tubes run between the wrist and the forearm actuator unit, reducing friction while preventing tendon slack. The 17 motors in the forearm are compactly bundled into a $98.4 \times 93.8 \times 155$ mm envelope. Each motor spool features a spiral groove with a 1.6 mm pitch, restricting spool radius variation to just 0.36%.

(h)-(j) Assembly view and prototype appearance of the complete hand, with a length of 200 mm and fingers symmetrically arranged at a $6^{\circ}$ opening angle.

captions.F6: Wrist and forearm actuator module. 32 tendons are routed through spring guide tubes and compactly gathered onto 17 motors equipped with helical grooved spools.

sections.heading: Faster-Than-Human Response and Dexterous Dual-Sided Grasping
sections.summary: This section covers thorough experimental performance evaluations. The hand achieved a 3.0% joint transmission error, a 13.2 Hz bandwidth, 29 N fingertip force, and 0.15 mm repeatability, while successfully performing Kapandji tests and all GRASP Taxonomy grasp patterns on both palmar and dorsal sides.
sections.details:
### IV-A Kinematics and Coupling Ratio Validation
Magnetic encoders were mounted at each joint to track sinusoidal command trajectories. The average error between commands and measured values was 3.9% for MCP FE, 1.6% for PIP FE, and 3.4% for MCP AbAd (overall average 3.0%), showing high tracking fidelity. The PIP-DIP coupling ratio was measured at 1:0.69, closely matching the design target of 3:2 (1:0.667) with an error of only 3.5%.

### IV-B Joint Transmission Bandwidth
Frequency response was measured across various amplitudes, yielding an average bandwidth of 15.2 Hz for MCP FE, 12.3 Hz for PIP FE, and 12.2 Hz for MCP AbAd (average 13.2 Hz). This is more than double the maximum human index finger tapping frequency (~6 Hz), enabling ultra-fast joint tracking well beyond human reflex limits.

### IV-C Core Hardware Performance (Force, Accuracy, Impact Resistance)
- **Fingertip Force**: Maximum fingertip force measured with a 6-axis force sensor was approximately 29 N. This exceeds the fingertip forces required for activities of daily living (ADL, typically under 15 N), providing a solid operational margin.
- **Positioning Repeatability**: Tested over 100 cycles. Pre-stretching the tendons to eliminate initial elongation dramatically improved maximum deviation: from 0.58 mm to 0.15 mm in FE joints, and from 0.19 mm to 0.02 mm in AbAd joints. This accuracy surpasses typical tendon-driven hands (around 0.2 to 1 mm).
- **Impact Resistance and Durability**: When struck forcefully with a hammer, the passive compliance (backdrivability) of the tendon drive absorbed the shock smoothly, returning to the commanded pose without damage. Continuous cycling over 5,400 cycles (3 hours) revealed no functional degradation.

### IV-D Dual-Sided Dexterity Evaluation (Kapandji & GRASP)
In Kapandji opposition testing, the thumb reached 8 out of 10 target positions (score: 8/10). In the GRASP Taxonomy test covering diverse grasps, the hand achieved 100% of all 33 grasp types on both the palmar and dorsal sides. Achieving identical scores on both sides proves that the dorsal side is not just an auxiliary feature, but possesses full dexterity equivalent to the palm.

### IV-E Bidirectional Manipulation Demonstrations
In an ambidextrous teleoperation demo, a single hand module switched between right-hand and left-hand configurations via vision to shake hands naturally with either human hand. Additional dynamic tasks demonstrated its unique bidirectional versatility, such as simultaneous dual-sided grasping (grasping an object on the front with the pinky while flipping the index finger to grasp another behind it) and catching balls thrown sequentially from the front and back without turning the wrist.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Next Steps: Moving Beyond Human Constraints
sections.summary: This section summarizes the achievements of the bidirectional hand as a lightweight, compact platform offering an expanded workspace. Future directions include adopting quasi-direct-drive motors, integrating tension sensors, and quantitatively assessing task time reductions gained from bidirectional operation.
sections.details:
This study developed a human-scale (200 mm, 220 g), 17-DoF bidirectional robotic hand using the proposed BATM, which eliminates return springs to actively drive positive and negative directions. By completing grasping operations across the neutral configuration on both palmar and dorsal sides, it breaks free from conventional human anatomical constraints and dramatically expands the operational workspace.

Experiments confirmed standout specifications: 13.2 Hz bandwidth, 29 N fingertip force, 0.15 mm repeatability, impact resilience, and 100% completion of all 33 GRASP grasp types on both sides. Practical utility was further validated through ambidextrous teleoperation and dynamic ball catching without wrist reorientation.

Room for improvement remains. First, the current motor reduction ratio is somewhat high; while fingertip force has ample margin, bandwidth is constrained. Adopting quasi-direct-drive (QDD) motors with lower gear ratios would enhance backdrivability and enable precise current-based torque control. Second, integrating spring-loaded tension sensors into tendon pathways to monitor tension and slack in real time, or introducing passive slack compensation mechanisms, is planned. Future work will quantitatively evaluate how much wrist travel distance and task completion time can be saved compared to conventional unidirectional hands.

takeaways: Rather than copying the human hand verbatim, giving it a bidirectionally symmetric structure eliminates redundant wrist rotations and boosts manipulation efficiency.
The BATM design, which winds two tendons in reverse from a single motor, achieves fully symmetric positive-negative drive across the neutral pose without return springs.
Careful geometric routing passing tendons directly through preceding joint rotation axes decouples joint motions in multi-DoF fingers.
Pre-stretching tendons to remove initial structural elongation enables high repeatability (up to 0.15 mm) in tendon-driven systems.
limitations: High gear reduction ratios provide ample fingertip force (29 N) but leave room for improvement in backdrivability and pure current-based torque control.
The hand currently lacks sensors to monitor tendon tension directly as well as passive automatic slack-compensation mechanisms.
Quantitative comparisons measuring task time and end-effector travel reductions during higher-level tasks versus conventional unidirectional hands remain for future work.
